doc.title: Arturo Sandoval interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 12, 2023

chapter: Career, recognition and jazz in America
title: Being a Latino musician: stereotypes and missing from jazz polls
summary: He says Latino musicians are typecast by origin and that he never appears on DownBeat trumpet lists despite 62 years of playing.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: It’s very interesting that musicians from countries other than America who get turned on to jazz, they seem, as you eloquently said, that it’s such a big part of your life and the struggles that you took to get there, I wonder if you appreciate it more than many American musicians?
I don’t think — hold on one second, bear with me, one second. Let me put the speaker on Bluetooth. Hold on, hold on.
Whatever you did just then made the video problematic.
I think now I’m connected. Talk to me please.
Yes. Okay. I think that yes, we’re back on, yeah.
Okay. Excellent. So we were talking about the struggles that you go through to arrive at a place in the music and you were talking about, you know, your travails and your life to get there.

Yeah. I’m going to tell you, it’s not easy to, when you’re a Latino person like me to really develop your career, especially in the classical or jazz music, because a lot of people are of a stereotype mentality and then when they hear you speaking or the color of © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

your skin or whatever, where you come from, they always associate you with the music of your country where you was born you know. And this is not fair. It is not fair at all. Because music is the only international language you know. It belongs to all human beings. It doesn’t matter where you was born or grew up you know. If you embrace the music and you really have a big passion and you develop some skill and some things, because you have dedication and you are disciplined, it should be recognized you know. I’ll give you an example. It’s funny that I’ve been reading all those magazines specializing in jazz, for example like DownBeat or a jazz magazine, all the things. When they put a list of jazz trumpeters I never appear in any of those kind of lists. They ignore me. Okay modesty apart, I laugh all the way to the bank no matter what. But it’s hard, because you say man I’m playing music for 62 years. I’m 74 now and I started playing music professionally when I was 12 years old, which means I’m playing music for 62 years non-stop you know, with a lot of passion, dedication, discipline, respect for the music and respect for the audience. And some people don’t believe that you deserve some kind of recognition, that’s your problem you know. I try as much as I can to do things that don’t affect my little brain you know. And what I do is keep practicing and trying to improve and trying to fix things that I feel I haven’t been doing maybe in the best way and then this has been my life for so many, many years you know. And I’m going to be like this until I retire or die I don’t know.
